Chapter Five: The Dangers of Religious Certainty and Division
Picture this—a family gathered around the dinner table, talking about the world beyond their window. The news is on, and stories of violence in faraway places drift through the room. The kids, trying to make sense of it all, ask, “Why do people fight over religion?” The parents, searching for answers, fall back on what they’ve always heard—“Our faith is true. Others just don’t understand.”
It’s a scene that plays out in homes everywhere. People wrestling with the reality of a world split by belief. And at the center of it is a powerful force: religious certainty. That deep conviction that our own faith is the only real truth—while everyone else must be lost, or even wrong.
But here’s something to pay attention to—most of us don’t realize just how easily this certainty can pull us apart. It often starts small. Maybe you skip a neighbor’s celebration because it doesn’t fit with your faith. Or a child is told not to spend time with classmates who believe something different. These little choices, repeated again and again, slowly build invisible walls around our communities. Over time, we stop seeing our neighbors as neighbors. Instead, they become strangers—sometimes, even threats.
And when those walls go up, the fallout can be huge. In some parts of the world, these divisions spark violence and war. In others, they lead to subtle, but painful discrimination—laws that single out minorities, or a culture where fear and suspicion take root. When we’re convinced that only our own path leads to the truth, it’s tough to build bridges or recognize the shared humanity in people who seem different from us.
But here’s the thing—sometimes, the walls come down. Think about a group of volunteers from all sorts of backgrounds, coming together after a natural disaster. In those moments, when everyone’s focused on helping, the differences that once felt so important just...fade. Suddenly, it’s obvious—what unites us is so much stronger than what keeps us apart.
Over time, you start to see that belief itself isn’t the real danger. The problem comes when we refuse to question—when faith is treated as untouchable, beyond criticism. That’s when it can turn into a kind of power, a tool that justifies almost anything. But if we’re willing to doubt, to ask the tough questions, that’s what helps us grow. That’s how societies move forward—together.
